title: Anders Behring Breivik
wiki_lead:
Anders Behring Breivik (born 13 February 1979) is a Norwegian mass murderer, white supremacist, and domestic terrorist who perpetrated the 2011 Norway attacks. A believer in the Great Replacement theory, he sought to combat perceived "Cultural Marxism" by detonating a car bomb at the Regjeringskvartalet (executive government quarter) in Oslo, then carrying out a mass shooting at a summer camp of the Labour Party's youth wing on the island of Utøya, in total killing 77 people and injuring over 323.
Found competent to stand trial, Breivik was tried in 2012, convicted on all charges, and sentenced to 21 years of preventive detention, with the possibility of extensions for as long as he is deemed to pose a danger to society.
At age 16, he was arrested for graffiti vandalism in Oslo. He later joined the anti-immigration Progress Party, chaired its Vest Oslo youth branch in 2002, and left in 2006. He joined a gun club in 2005. A company he founded later went bankrupt, and he reported no income in 2009. He financed the attacks with about €130,000 using credit cards.
On the day of the attacks, Breivik distributed a compendium titled 2083: A European Declaration of Independence, outlining his ideology. In it, he opposed Islam, blamed feminism for a perceived European "cultural suicide", and called for the deportation of Muslims from Europe, stating that publicising the text was a primary motive.
Two teams of forensic psychiatrists evaluated Breivik before the trial. While the first diagnosed paranoid schizophrenia, a second concluded he was not psychotic at the time of the attacks and instead had narcissistic personality disorder and antisocial personality disorder.
Breivik has since filed multiple legal challenges against the Norwegian Correctional Service under the European Convention on Human Rights regarding his confinement. A partial ruling in his favour in 2016 was overturned on appeal, and later challenges, including a 2024 case on prison isolation, were unsuccessful.

Early life
Breivik was born in Oslo on 13 February 1979, the son of Jens Breivik (born 1935), a civil economist, who worked as a diplomat for the Norwegian Embassy in London and later in Paris, and Wenche Elisabeth Behring (1946–2013), a nursing assistant. He has a maternal half-sister named Elisabeth, and three paternal half-siblings: Erik, Jan, and Nina. Breivik lived in London until aged one, when his parents divorced. His family name is Breivik, and his middle name, Behring, is his mother's maiden name. In 2017, it was reported he had changed his legal name to Fjotolf Hansen.

When Breivik was aged four, and living in Oslo's Frogner borough, two reports were filed expressing concern about his mental health. A psychologist in one report made a note of the boy's peculiar smile, suggesting it was not anchored in his emotions but was rather a deliberate response to his environment. grok_lead: Anders Behring Breivik (born 13 February 1979) is a Norwegian terrorist who executed coordinated attacks on 22 July 2011, beginning with a car bomb detonation in Oslo's government quarter that killed eight people and injured dozens, followed by a mass shooting at the Norwegian Labour Party youth camp on UtÃ¸ya island, where he killed 69 individuals, predominantly teenagers and young adults, for a total of 77 deaths and over 300 injuries. Prior to the assaults, Breivik self-published and distributed a 1,500-page compendium titled 2083: A European Declaration of Independence, in which he articulated grievances against multiculturalism, Muslim immigration, and policies he attributed to "cultural Marxism," particularly those advanced by the Labour Party, framing the attacks as a defensive strike against the erosion of European cultural and national identity. Breivik meticulously prepared for the operation over several years, acquiring materials for the fertilizer-based bomb, obtaining firearms legally, and undergoing physical training while operating under a fabricated cover as a business enterprise. In his manifesto and subsequent trial testimony, he positioned himself as a knight templar resisting what he described as an ongoing civilizational conflict, explicitly targeting the Labour youth gathering due to the party's role in promoting immigration policies he viewed as enabling demographic and cultural displacement. The attacks, the deadliest in Norway since World War II, prompted national reckoning with extremism, security lapses, and ideological undercurrents, though Breivik rejected insanity defenses to ensure his political rationale received public airing. Following a 10-week trial in 2012, Breivik was adjudged criminally sane and convicted on charges of gross terrorism and premeditated murder, receiving Norway's severest penalty: 21 years' preventive detention, extendable indefinitely if societal risk persists, a regime he has since challenged in courts alleging human rights violations from isolation conditions.
